questions.question: How do you use fmt.Sprintf and what are the common format verbs?
questions.title: Fmt Sprintf
questions.direct_answer: fmt.Sprintf(format, args...) returns a formatted string: %s strings, %d ints, %f floats, %v anything (the always-works verb), %q quoted, %T type. Sprintf→string, Printf→stdout, Fprintf→any Writer.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Fmt Sprintf beyond memorized syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the concept to a small production example and state its complexity or failure mode.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Recall: fmt.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Sprintf builds a string from a format and arguments:

```go
name, age := "Al", 30
s := fmt.Sprintf("Hi %s, you are %d", name, age)
// "Hi Al, you are 30"
```

The verbs worth knowing cold:

- %s — strings (and Stringers)
- %d — integers
- %f — floats (%.2f for precision)
- %v — default format for ANY value — always works
- %q — quoted Go syntax: strings get \"go\"
- %T — the TYPE — debugging gold
- %x — hex

```go
fmt.Sprintf("%q %x %v", "go", 255, []int{1,2})
// "go" ff [1 2]  — executed
```

%v is the safety verb — never fails to render SOMETHING (structs as {a b c}, nil as <nil>) — right default for logs, wrong for user-facing exact control.

The family: Sprintf → string. Printf → stdout. Fprintf → any io.Writer (files, buffers, network). Errorf → an error (different family, same verbs — the %w special case lives there).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    F[format string] --> P[runtime parse]
    P --> D[verb dispatch]
    D --> R[result string]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The format mini-language beyond verbs — the interview follow-up: %10s pads width 10 (right-aligned), %-10s left, %08d zero-pads, %.2f float precision, % x spaces hex bytes. Width and precision are the two numbers; flags are letters.

The %v family: %+v adds field NAMES ({Name:Al Age:30} — the debugging upgrade), %#v prints Go-source representation (map[string]int{\"a\":1} — copy-pasteable). Three detail levels, one character apart.

The performance contract: Sprintf parses the format at RUNTIME every call — reflection over args, verb dispatch. ~3-5x an Itoa path, allocation-heavy — fine for UI/errors, wrong in hot loops. The escapes: strconv (no format parsing), plain concatenation for fixed shapes, Builder for accumulation. If it's in a loop or request path, measure — Sprintf is usually the first flag.

Errorf's special case: %w is a WRAP directive (fmt.Errorf("ctx: %w", err) chains the error) — Sprintf and Errorf share the mini-language, diverge on that one verb. Knowing the divergence is depth.

questions.question: What is the difference between %v, %s, and %q in Go format strings?
questions.title: When would you use Fmt Sprintf in a real project
questions.direct_answer: %v: default rendering of any value. %s: the string/Stringer form. %q: the value as Go SOURCE — quoted, with escapes visible. Use %v to debug, %s for text, %q to log untrusted content safely.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: %v: default rendering of any value. %s: the string/Stringer form. %q: the value as Go SOURCE — quoted, with escapes visible. Use %v to debug, %s for text, %q to.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Three verbs, three contracts, one comparison:

```go
fmt.Sprintf("%v", "go")  // go
fmt.Sprintf("%s", "go")  // go
fmt.Sprintf("%q", "go")  // "go" — quoted

fmt.Sprintf("%v %s %q", 'g', 'g', 'g')
// 103 g 'g'   — %v: the NUMBER, %s: the character, %q: quoted
```

Executed. The differences that matter:

%v renders the DEFAULT form — never fails. For a rune (int32), that's the NUMBER (103). For structs, {Field Values}. For nil pointers, <nil>. The debug/log verb.

%s renders the string-or-Stringer form: strings, []byte as text, anything with String() gets it called. A rune under %s shows the CHARACTER.

%q renders the SOURCE form: strings become \"...\" with internal quotes/escapes ESCAPED, runes become '...'. The safe verb for LOGGING UNTRUSTED DATA — a %v of input containing quotes or ANSI escapes injects into your terminal; %q neutralizes it.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    V[v - default: any value]
    S[s - text or Stringer]
    Q[q - quoted source form]
    R[rune 103] --> |as v| 103
    R --> |as s| g
    R --> |as q| quoted g
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The rendering pipeline — the interfaces %v and %s consult: both check for Stringer (String()) and error (Error()); %s additionally handles string/[]byte natively. For values with NEITHER, %s silently falls back to %v's default — why %s on an int 'works' (42) and the difference only surfaces with runes (the int32-that-is-a-rune: %v number, %s character).

%q's implementation per kind: strings → strconv.Quote (double-quoted, escapes: \", \\, \n, \xNN for non-printables); runes → strconv.QuoteRune ('g', 'é'); integers → %d (nothing to quote). 'Quote if quotable, default otherwise.' The escaping table is the security story: terminal escapes render as source form — log injection (the log4j-style newline-escape pattern) is neutralized at the verb level.

When to reach for each, one line per context: logs → %v (+%v for structs); user-visible text → %s (or direct print); log fields with untrusted content → %q (injection-proof); type debugging → %T next to %v — the standard 'what IS this' pair.

questions.question: What is the difference between fmt.Sprintf and strconv.Itoa, and when should you use each?
questions.title: a common mistake when using Fmt Sprintf
questions.direct_answer: Itoa: int→string only, no format parsing — fast. Sprintf: full format language, any types — 3-5x slower. Hot paths: Itoa. Formatted output: Sprintf.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Recall: Itoa: int→string only, no format parsing — fast.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Both turn an int into a string; the difference is generality vs cost:

```go
n := 42
strconv.Itoa(n)              // "42" — direct, fast
fmt.Sprintf("%d", n)         // "42" — parses format, reflects, formats
```

Sprintf's machinery: parse the format string at runtime, reflect over the argument's type, dispatch the verb, allocate the result. It's a full mini-interpreter per call. Itoa is a tight decimal-encoding routine — no format, no reflection, one small allocation.

The performance folklore is real: benchmarks consistently show Sprintf ~3-5x Itoa for the simple int case, more with multiple args. In a hot path (per-request logging, tight loops, serialization), that compounds.

When each is right: Itoa (and the strconv family — FormatInt, FormatFloat, Atoi) when the conversion is EXACTLY one value → one string with no surrounding text. Sprintf when you're composing — text + values + formatting (widths, precision, multiple args) — the moment there's a sentence to build, the format language earns its cost.

The hybrid most real code uses: build the static parts with concatenation or Builder, use strconv for the value insertions — the pattern every fast logger uses internally.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    I[strconv.Itoa - tight loop, one alloc]
    F[Sprintf - parse format + reflect + alloc]
    I --> |hot path| FAST[3-5x faster]
    F --> |composition| GEN[the format language]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why the cost gap is structural, not incidental: Sprintf's runtime format parsing means — per call — a scan of the format string, a type-switch on each argument (via reflection for interface-boxed args), verb dispatch, and a fresh allocation for the output. Itoa's path: one if-chain for the sign, a loop of divide-by-10 digit extraction, one allocation. The reflection and parsing are Sprintf's whole value (any type, any format) and its whole overhead — the same generality/cost trade the entire fmt package makes (Print vs manual strconv: identical story).

The Append family as the zero-allocation tier: strconv.AppendInt(buf, n, 10) writes into a caller-provided []byte — no string allocation at all. encoding/json's int encoder is literally this call — the hot path inside the standard library skips fmt entirely. For your own hot paths, the progression is: Sprintf (readable) → Itoa/FormatInt (one value) → AppendInt into a reused buffer (zero alloc, maximal ceremony).

The API-design note interviewers reward: Go's own hot-path code (encoding/json, strconv-based loggers) never uses fmt for inner loops — fmt is the presentation layer (user-facing strings, errors, top-level logs), and the ecosystem's performance discipline is 'fmt at the edges, strconv/append in the cores.' Matching that split in your own code is the sign of knowing both tools.

questions.question: How do you format floats in Go without surprises?
questions.title: compare Fmt Sprintf with an alternative
questions.direct_answer: %.2f for fixed decimals: fmt.Sprintf("%.2f", 3.14159) → "3.14". strconv.FormatFloat for the fast path. Beware: binary floats can't represent 0.1 exactly — format for display, never compare formatted output for equality.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Recall: %.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The fixed-decimal form is %.Nf:

```go
fmt.Sprintf("%.2f", 3.14159)   // "3.14"
fmt.Sprintf("%.0f", 2.7)      // "3" — rounds
fmt.Sprintf("%8.2f", 3.14159)  // "    3.14" — width 8, right-aligned
```

The scientific form is %e ("3.14e+00"), the shortest-round-trip is %g (picks f or e by magnitude — what fmt.Println uses by default).

The representation surprise every float formatter must know: binary floating point can't exactly represent most decimal fractions — 0.1 is stored as 0.1000000000000000055511... The DEFAULT rendering shows this: fmt.Println(0.1) prints 0.1 (Go's %g picks the shortest form that round-trips — reading it back gives the same bits), but naive %.20f exposes the truth: 0.10000000000000000555.

The consequences: %.2f is a DISPLAY format (rounding for humans); comparing formatted strings for float equality is wrong (rounds differently at boundaries); and money — the classic case — should be integer cents (int64), formatted by dividing at display time. The rounding Go uses for %.Nf is correct decimal rounding of the binary value — but the value itself carries the representation error.

For exact decimal arithmetic: math/big.Float or a decimal library (or the int-cents pattern). For display: %.Nf with the knowledge that it's display.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    F2[%.2f - fixed decimals]
    G[%g - shortest round-trip]
    B[binary 0.1] --> |actual value| T[0.10000000000000000555...]
    T --> |%g| P[0.1 - shortest that round-trips]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why %g prints 0.1 as '0.1' — the shortest-round-trip algorithm: Go's float formatting tries successively shorter decimal representations until it finds one that, PARSED BACK, yields the identical float64 bits. 0.1's nearest representable double is 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827... — but '0.1' parses to exactly that double, so '0.1' wins. This is Ryu-style shortest-printing (modern Go uses a variant) — the guarantee: the printed form round-trips exactly, so logging a float and parsing the log NEVER corrupts the value.

%.Nf's mechanics vs %g: %.Nf is positional decimal formatting with rounding at the Nth place (correct half-away-from-zero on the binary value's decimal expansion). %g adapts (fixed or scientific, by exponent range, defaulting to shortest). %e is always scientific. The three cover the display space: fixed (%f), scientific (%e), adaptive-short (%g).

The money pattern, fully: float amounts accumulate error (0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004 — the famous demonstration), so amounts store as int64 cents/units; display divides: fmt.Sprintf("%d.%02d", cents/100, cents%100) — integer math all the way, formatting only at the edge. Interviewers probe this as 'how do you handle money in Go' — the answer is never 'floats with %.2f'; it's int cents + the divide-at-display idiom, with the float path reserved for physical/scientific quantities where the representation error is smaller than measurement error.

questions.question: What is the difference between Printf, Sprintf, Fprintf, and Errorf in Go?
questions.title: debug a problem involving Fmt Sprintf
questions.direct_answer: All share the format verbs. Printf → stdout. Sprintf → returns a string. Fprintf → any io.Writer. Errorf → returns an error (and its %w wraps). Choose by DESTINATION.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Recall: All share the format verbs.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
One format mini-language, four destinations:

```go
fmt.Printf("Hi %s\n", name)          // → stdout
s := fmt.Sprintf("Hi %s", name)      // → string (returned)
fmt.Fprintf(w, "Hi %s", name)        // → any io.Writer: file, buffer, network
err := fmt.Errorf("Hi %s: %w", name, cause)  // → error value
```

The verbs are identical across all four — %s, %d, %v, %q, %T — learn once, use everywhere.

The choosing rule is the destination: console output → Printf; building a string for later use (API messages, descriptions) → Sprintf; writing to anything that isn't stdout (log files, HTTP responses, bytes.Buffer, sockets) → Fprintf (that's the io.Writer interface — the same one bytes.Buffer, files, and network connections implement); creating an error with context → Errorf.

Errorf's special verb: %w. In Errorf ONLY, %w embeds the wrapped error and links the Unwrap chain (errors.Is/As traverse it). In Sprintf, %w is invalid (a placeholder mishap — it prints %!w(...)). That single divergence is why Errorf isn't just 'Sprintf that returns an error' — it's the errors-package integration point.

The perf note that carries over from the Sprintf topic: all four parse the format at runtime — the cost profile is shared. Printf to a buffered writer, Sprintf in hot loops — the same discipline applies per destination.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P[Printf - stdout]
    S[Sprintf - string]
    F[Fprintf - any io.Writer]
    E[Errorf - error value]
    E --> W[w - wraps, only in Errorf]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The Writer abstraction behind Fprintf is the whole story of why four functions exist at all: fmt prints to io.Writer (the two-word interface: Write([]byte) (int, error)). Printf is literally Fprintf(os.Stdout, ...) — a convenience binding. Sprintf is Fprintf into a private buffer whose String() is returned. The destination is pluggable — which is how fmt composes with the entire IO ecosystem: a bytes.Buffer (capture for testing), a file (logging), a hash (the md5 of the formatted form), a network conn — one formatting engine, any sink.

Errorf's %w, mechanically: the format engine in Errorf scans for %w; on finding it, the wrapped error is stored in a wrapError struct alongside the formatted message, and that struct implements Unwrap() → the cause. errors.Is/As walk that chain. %v would embed the cause's TEXT in the message string — no link, no chain. The one-verb divergence is the entire errors-as-values architecture's integration with formatting — which is why 'use %w not %v when wrapping' is the rule (the errors topic covers the semantics; here the point is the FORMAT engine's role).

The testing idiom worth naming: capturing Fprintf output for assertions — write to bytes.Buffer, format into it, assert buf.String(). Because Sprintf also exists, the choice is style: Sprintf for one-shot expected strings, Fprintf-to-buffer when emulating a writer-driven component (a logger that takes io.Writer — test it with a buffer; the same code path as production). That testability is io.Writer's second dividend — the first was composability.
